newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Children come before parents for EU mediator.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Children come before parents for EU mediator.

text.p: "Excuse me, I just want to take this," said the European Parliament's Mediator for Abducted Children, Mary Banotti, as she interrupted our interview to answer a telephone call from a highly distressed Italian mother.

The mother's desperate plea for help to retrieve her four children from a Swiss orphanage underlines a point the former Irish nurse had just made -- before you marry or have children with someone from another country, think twice.

As the woman charged by the EU assembly to help resolve tug-of-love quarrels which end in kidnap when parents separate, Banotti has heard her fair share of holiday romances which started on a sunny beach and ended in nightmare.

"My biggest advice is when people meet someone from a different country before they marry or have children that they try to spend some time in each other's country," Banotti, a Euro-MP for Ireland's Fine Gael party, told Reuters.

"When it's a lovely sunny beach or they are under the moon they don't think about the issues. You can see a difference when you see people in their own homes. On that basis I advise people to marry the boy next door," she said, admitting that she herself married an Italian.

With an anxious eye on the fax for news from Western Samoa in the Pacific, where a court case on Monday could determine whether a German woman, Christine Wagner, retrieves her nine-year-old son Tom, Banotti says the last people parents usually think about when they abduct are the children.
"The motivation is a mixture of love, rage, revenge and fear," she says.
If you are afraid that your children are about to be abducted, she advises -- hide their passports, keep recent photographs, even get their fingerprints taken.
STAYING WITHIN THE LAW
Banotti, who dealt with 18 abduction cases last year, says she never steps outside the law in her bid to help mothers or fathers who have lost their children.

What she can do is give advice and lend the EU's authority when small local courts -- often in holiday resorts in Spain and Greece and lacking in specialist knowledge -- or the police refuse to take a case seriously, thinking they have just another domestic row on their hands.

"We never break the law. The law is the Hague convention which says the custody must be decided in the usual country of residence. They know that I'm going to be honest about how I deal with it and professional," she said.
But she says the law is not tight enough and is applied laxly, particularly in Spain, Greece and Germany.
In a review of the convention this spring she will push for a system of specialised courts to deal with cases quickly and set standards of training for lawyers.
A HAPPY HOMECOMING FOR IRISH TWINS
When Banotti's office telephoned Ireland's Catherine Hughes to say her four-year-old twins had been found and that she should hop on a plane to France she could hardly believe her ears.
An earlier dash to France had ended in disappointment.
The children's French father Claude Blanc had moved them to Switzerland and revealed where they were only when he was arrested by French police.

Banotti and her assistant helped the mother deal with the local court and police and looked after the twins as they ran round the airport as four months of sleepless nights and financial worry took their toll on their mother.

"When I was told that they had been found Mary Banotti came with me from Ireland to Marseille. I said I should feel very very happy but I was very very nervous, I was crying. She told me what I was feeling was normal.

"I found it very consoling -- she's a very strong person, a very sympathetic person. What happened to me in four months it seemed to be four years. It's an experience I would not wish for any woman or any man," Hughes said.
As a mediator it is Banotti's role to treat both parents equally and put the children first.
"What impressed me is that their priority is the children, not me, not Claude," Hughes said.
BRITISH MOTHER THREATENED WITH DEATH

When Briton Pamela Hamilton went to a Tunisian court on Tuesday this week to plead that her former husband return her nine-year-old twin boys she knew that in 30 years not a single woman had retrieved a child from the country.

But with her 14-year-old daughter suffering from depression back home and no chance of seeing or telephoning her boys -- abducted after the father failed to return them after a 12-hour visit -- she knew she had to go to the expense and distress of a court case in a foreign country.

She told Reuters ahead of the court case that she turned to Banotti for advice after receiving little help from the British government. Banotti then established contacts with Tunisia's ambassador in Brussels.
"I'm very pessimistic but I can't go to the European Court until they refuse. It's the first step," Hamilton said.

Her brother later told Reuters by telephone that Hamilton was beaten up in the street by her former husband, who announced in a brief court hearing he would kill her. The Tunisian court told her to return on February 18, he said.
